headline: Valiant Rock at 4.1 Knots: Wire Line Bass Hold Through the Push
subhead: A steep thermal split across the Sound is stacking stripers in the cold water at The Race while the west side goes quiet — here's where and when to fish the window.
body_markdown:
Valiant Rock ran 4.1 knots on Thursday's max ebb, and that's the number that tells you everything about this week. Slack came in tight — about eleven minutes either side of 11:20 — and in that window I put three fish over 30 inches in the boat on wire line and a white bucktail worked off the north face of the rock in 38 feet. Miss that window by fifteen minutes and you're fighting current instead of fishing it. That's The Race in July — it doesn't give you much room, but it gives you fish if you're precise about it.

Here's why this window matters more than usual right now. New London is sitting at 66.4 degrees. Kings Point, forty-some miles west, is reading 71.2. That's a five-degree spread across one body of water, and it's not closing anytime soon with this heat. Stripers don't love water in the low 70s in July — they get sluggish, push deep, or bail for cooler structure. The eastern Sound, where I live and fish, is still cold enough to hold them tight to bottom in the rips. That's the whole story this week: the fish that would normally be spreading out into the Sound's open water are pinned to Race Rock, Valiant Rock, and the Gut because the current there keeps things cold and oxygenated even as the surface cooks.

The bite itself has been technical, not a blitz. I'm not going to oversell it — you have to work for these fish right now. Wire line, 60-foot drops off the downtide side of Valiant on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most consistent producer, bucktails in the 2 to 3-ounce range, white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of pork rind or a Fin-S trailer when the current really starts hauling. Depths from 35 to 50 feet. The fish are holding low, right on the boulder fields, and you need enough lead to feel bottom through 4 knots of water or you're just trolling air above them. Slack itself is short and sweet — five, maybe ten minutes of genuinely fishable water before the tide turns and starts building the other way — but that's when the bigger fish, the 34-to-40-inch class, come off the rock faces to feed. I've had my best two fish of the week come in that exact window at Valiant, both on the drop of the tide right before the flood takes hold.

Plum Gut has been a bluefish story more than a bass story this week. Fresh bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, 20 to 30 feet off Orient Point on the outgoing, has been putting solid 8 to 12-pound blues in the boat pretty reliably, along with the occasional bass mixed in on the same baits. If you want the bass specifically out of the Gut, work the eddy lines on the Long Island side with a 3-ounce diamond jig on the drop, tight to bottom where the current stacks bait against the drop-off.

Fluke have been steady but not spectacular on the sand flats behind the Sluiceway and off Little Gull. Drifting 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 30 feet, outgoing tide, has produced keeper-class fish to 22 inches with enough shorts mixed in that you're culling, not scrambling. Black sea bass around Race Rock and the boulder piles off Great Gull have been a bright spot — squid strips and Gulp jigs dropped straight down on structure in 40 to 60 feet are filling coolers, and that fishery's been the most dependable thing out here all month.

On false albacore and bonito — it's too early, and I'd rather tell you that straight than sell you a fantasy. The open ocean side is reading 72.9 at the NY Bight buoy with a building 2.3-foot swell, which tells me warmer water is pushing toward the Race from the south. That's the setup that eventually pulls albies through Plum Gut and into the Sluiceway, usually by early-to-mid August once the bay anchovies and silversides show up thick. I'll be running epoxy jigs and checking the rips daily starting the last week of July, but right now there's no bait signature or surface activity out there worth a special trip.

Looking ahead: the tide cycle is building toward bigger swings over the next several days, which should tighten these slack windows even further and could push more bass up onto the rock faces during the transition periods. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of a strong ebb at Valiant Rock, wire line down to bottom, and I'd have the epoxy jigs rigged and ready in case anything shows on the surface at the Gut on the way back in. The bite's there, but it's a precision game right now — miss the window, miss the fish.
